subject: Engineering Mathematics
summary: analytic functions and the Cauchy–Riemann equations, harmonic conjugates, singularities and residues, Cauchy's integral theorem and formula, Laurent series; Newton–Raphson and bisection, the trapezoidal and Simpson's rules, and Euler, Heun and Runge–Kutta methods for ODEs

questions.text: With z = x + iy, which of the following functions is NOT analytic?
solution: Concept: f = u + iv is analytic in a region only if ux = vy and uy = −vx hold there.
For x² + iy²: u<sub>x</sub> = 2x, v<sub>y</sub> = 2y, so C–R hold only on the line y = x.
A function differentiable only on a line has no neighbourhood of analyticity: (D).
Exam tip: Any function built from z alone (polynomials, ez, sin z) is analytic; anything that needs x and y separately is suspect.

questions.text: f(z) = u + iv is analytic with u = x³ − 3xy² and v(0, 0) = 0. The value of v at the point (1, 2) is ______
solution: Concept: Find the harmonic conjugate from the C–R equations.
v<sub>y</sub> = u<sub>x</sub> = 3x² − 3y² → v = 3x²y − y³ + g(x)
v<sub>x</sub> = 6xy + g′(x) must equal −u<sub>y</sub> = 6xy, so g = const = 0
Exam tip: Milne–Thomson shortcut: f′(z) = ux(z, 0) − i uy(z, 0) = 3z², so f = z³.

questions.text: The residue of f(z) = e<sup>2z</sup>/(z − 1)² at z = 1 is
solution: Concept: For a pole of order 2 at a: Res = d/dz[(z − a)²f(z)] at z = a.
(z − 1)²f = e<sup>2z</sup>; its derivative is 2e<sup>2z</sup>
At z = 1: Res = 2e² (A)
Exam tip: For order m: Res = [1/(m − 1)!] dm−1/dzm−1[(z − a)mf] at a.

questions.text: Let C be the circle |z| = 3, traversed anticlockwise, and I = ∮<sub>C</sub> (z² + 1)/[z(z − 2)] dz. The value of I/(πi) is ______
solution: Concept: Residue theorem: I = 2πi × (sum of residues inside C).
Both z = 0 and z = 2 lie inside |z| = 3.
I = 2πi × 2 = 4πi, so I/(πi) = 4
Exam tip: Always check which singularities lie inside the contour before adding residues.

questions.text: The function f(z) = e<sup>1/z</sup> has at z = 0
solution: Concept: Classify by the principal part (negative powers) of the Laurent series.
e<sup>1/z</sup> = 1 + 1/z + 1/(2!z²) + 1/(3!z³) + … has infinitely many negative powers.
So z = 0 is an essential singularity (C); its residue is 1.
Exam tip: Finite number of negative powers → pole (order = highest power); none → removable.

questions.text: The cube root of 20 is found by the Newton–Raphson method applied to f(x) = x³ − 20, starting from x<sub>0</sub> = 3. The value of x<sub>1</sub> (round off to four decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: xn+1 = xn − f(xn)/f′(xn).
Exam tip: The true root is 2.7144; one more step gives 2.7146, showing quadratic convergence.

questions.text: Simpson's 1/3 rule can be applied directly (without combining with another rule) only when the interval is divided into
solution: Concept: Simpson's 1/3 rule fits a parabola through each pair of strips (three points).
So the number of strips n must be even (B).
Simpson's 3/8 rule uses cubics over groups of three strips (n a multiple of 3).
Exam tip: I ≈ (h/3)[f0 + 4(odd ordinates) + 2(even interior ordinates) + fn].

questions.text: The integral of sin x from 0 to π is evaluated by the trapezoidal rule with four equal strips (h = π/4). The value obtained (round off to three decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: I ≈ (h/2)[f0 + 2(f1 + f2 + f3) + f4].
Exam tip: The exact value is 2; for a concave function the trapezoidal rule underestimates (chords lie below the curve).

questions.text: For Euler's explicit method with step size h, the local truncation error and the global error are of order
solution: Concept: Euler's method keeps only the first two Taylor terms: y(x + h) = y + hy′ + (h²/2)y″ + …
Error per step ∝ h²; over (b − a)/h steps the errors add up to ∝ h.
So local O(h²), global O(h) (A): Euler is a first-order method.
Exam tip: Heun/modified Euler: global O(h²); classical RK4: global O(h⁴).

questions.text: The classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta method is used for dy/dx = −2xy, y(0) = 1, with one step h = 0.2. The value of y at x = 0.2 (round off to four decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: y1 = y0 + (h/6)(k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4).
Exam tip: The exact solution e−x² gives 0.960789 at x = 0.2: RK4 agrees to six decimals.

questions.text: Let C be the circle |z| = 1 traversed anticlockwise, as shown. The value of ∮<sub>C</sub> z²/(z − 3) dz is
solution: Concept: Cauchy–Goursat theorem: the integral of a function analytic inside and on a closed contour is zero.
The only singularity, z = 3, lies outside |z| = 1.
So the integrand is analytic on and inside C and the integral is 0 (D).
Exam tip: 2πi × 9 would be the answer only if the contour enclosed z = 3 (e.g. |z| = 4).

questions.text: The integral of e<sup>−x²</sup> from 0 to 1 is evaluated by Simpson's 1/3 rule with four equal strips (h = 0.25). The value obtained (round off to four decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: I ≈ (h/3)[f0 + 4(f1 + f3) + 2f2 + f4].
Exam tip: The exact value is 0.746824: Simpson's rule with only four strips is already accurate to four decimals.

questions.text: The function f(z) = (sin z)/z⁴ has at z = 0
solution: Concept: Expand and read off the highest negative power.
The highest negative power is z−3: a pole of order 3 (C), with residue −1/6.
Exam tip: Order of pole = (order of zero of denominator) − (order of zero of numerator) = 4 − 1.

questions.text: The bisection method is applied to f(x) = x³ − x − 1 on the interval [1, 2]. The third midpoint computed (m<sub>3</sub>, round off to three decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Keep the half-interval at whose ends f changes sign.
m3 = 1.375 (f = 0.2246 > 0, so the next interval is [1.25, 1.375])
Exam tip: After n bisections the error bound is (b − a)/2n; the true root is 1.3247.

questions.text: In polar form, z = re<sup>iθ</sup> and f = u(r, θ) + iv(r, θ), the Cauchy–Riemann equations are
opts: u<sub>r</sub> = r v<sub>θ</sub> and v<sub>r</sub> = −r u<sub>θ</sub>
solution: Concept: Equate f′ computed along the radial and the circumferential directions.
Radial: f′ = e<sup>−iθ</sup>(u<sub>r</sub> + iv<sub>r</sub>); circumferential: f′ = e<sup>−iθ</sup>(v<sub>θ</sub> − iu<sub>θ</sub>)/r
Hence ur = vθ/r and vr = −uθ/r (B).
Exam tip: Check with f = z² = r²e2iθ: ur = 2r cos 2θ = (1/r)(2r² cos 2θ) = vθ/r.
